articles.title: Rising mortgage rates and home prices sidelining buyers but now is the time to purchase, report says
articles.text:
Rising mortgage rates and home prices sidelining buyers but now is the time to purchase, report says - WBEZ Chicago
Potential homebuyers and their agents wait outside of an open house in June for a one-bedroom condo in Lake View.
Zubaer Khan/Sun-Times
Housing
Money
Rising mortgage rates and home prices sidelining buyers but now is the time to purchase, report says
October is the best time for potential homebuyers in Chicago to snag a deal, according to a new Redfin report. But it comes amid an inventory crunch and rising mortgage rates.
By
Abby Miller
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Hopeful buyers poured into open houses across the North Side over the summer. Some real estate agents reported nearly 100 people touring their listings.
But Keller Williams One Chicago Realtor Tommy Choi had less than 30 people recently visit his listing in Lincoln Park, one of the city’s hottest real estate markets.
There were four offers on the townhome, though a few months ago he would’ve expected about 10. While the property sold for nearly $100,000 over its asking price, it would’ve likely commanded much higher in the summer — when the market was more competitive and prompted bidding wars across Chicago.
The housing market slows down in the fall, as children return to school and families prep for the upcoming holiday season. But it also means buyers — who’ve struggled for months to find a home in their budget — could score a discount.
A Redfin report found October is the best time for homebuyers to score a deal in Chicago, as well as 15 other major cities such as Boston, Philadelphia and Orlando. “The seasonal sweet spot represents the time when discounts off a home’s original asking price — through price cuts or negotiations — are typically near their highest,” according to the September report.
“The sellers that are still struggling to get offers come October are going to be more willing to accept an offer below listing price or to lower the price themselves — or offer other sweeteners,” Redfin Chief Economist Daryl Fairweather said. “It’s really because they want to get things done. They don’t want to have this home sale hanging over their heads going into the holidays. As a buyer, that means that you’re going to be having sellers that are more willing to negotiate with you than they would have been in summer or spring.”
October has historically offered better opportunities for homebuyers, data from Illinois Realtors shows. Between 2021 and 2025, Chicago’s median sale price in October was lower compared to June, typically the peak buying month, averaging a 10% decline. The trade association found a similar trend with a home’s days on market — the longer a home sits, the more willing sellers are to accept price cuts or toss in other conditions to close a sale.
Ezekiel Morris, managing broker of EXIT Strategy Realty/EMA Management, said affordability and a lack of inventory have been the defining themes of Chicago’s housing market this year. He primarily serves the South Side and has seen some buyers broaden their search from North Side neighborhoods to the south.
He sees more opportunities this fall for buyers, especially those who qualify for down payment assistance and similar programs that can boost their budget.
“There’s deals at every level,” Morris said.
While October can be a period of relief for buyers, prices have been rising — even in October. And mortgage rates have also climbed.
Redfin data shows in October 2020, the median sale price for a home in the Chicago metro area was $275,000. That figure soared by about 33% to $366,500 in October 2025. When compared to the market’s peak time, data shows the median sale price in June 2020 was $269,000 and jumped to $407,000 in June 2025 — a roughly 51% increase.
Fairweather said nationally, a record number of buyers have backed out of purchasing homes, and pending home sales have plunged as rising mortgage rates cause people to change their mind.
September saw pending home sales in the U.S. drop 4% from August and 8.6% year over year. It’s also the first time in three years that pending home sales declined in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metro markets. Chicago declined 5.8% year over year and the share of deals under contract that fell through was 14.1%, Redfin said.
Tracking pending home sales can give real-time insight into the housing market and quickly reflect the impact of rising mortgage rates on consumers.
The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 7.40%, the same as last week, Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.27%.
“Chicago is kind of different from the national market because there aren’t enough sellers … and there are more buyers in Chicago compared to other parts of the country,” Fairweather said. “But even so, October is the best time to negotiate because those sellers that haven’t sold yet are going to be willing to lower their price. But the high mortgage rates have just priced out a lot of people who just can’t work it under these higher mortgage rates. So if you’re still in the market right now, then you really aren’t facing much buyer competition at all — and the sellers are willing to work with you.”
Dan Gjeldum, executive vice president of mortgage lending at CrossCountry Mortgage, thinks interest rates have been increasing faster than normal this year. He said it’s partly due to the war in Iran, which is impacting everything from inflation to oil prices.
“Inflation’s the arch enemy of mortgage rates, or interest rates in general,” he said.
Mortgage rate increases have reset the expectations of many buyers, Gjeldum said. CrossCountry has also seen fewer prospective clients than usual, and Gjeldum has been reaching out to pre-approved clients to discuss how the rate changes may impact their monthly mortgage payment.

articles.title: Old Town School of Folk teacher Ted Johnson, who shared ‘magic’ of music with decades of students, has died
articles.text:
Old Town School of Folk teacher Ted Johnson, who shared ‘magic’ of music with decades of students, has died - WBEZ Chicago
Theodore “Ted” Johnson was an ongoing presence at the legendary music school throughout his life, first as an instructor for more than 40 years and then returning as a student for nearly 20 more years.
Courtesy of the Johnson family
Obituaries
Music
Arts & Culture
Old Town School of Folk teacher Ted Johnson, who shared ‘magic’ of music with decades of students, has died
An Old Town instructor since day one, the Evanston-raised Johnson taught guitar, banjo and, in the late 1990s, even yodeling to students through a groundbreaking technique developed to democratize music instruction.
By
Mark Guarino
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Theodore “Ted” Johnson, an instructor at the Old Town School of Folk Music since the day it opened in 1957, died Saturday. He was 98.
Johnson was an ongoing presence at the legendary music school throughout his life, first as an instructor for more than 40 years and then returning as a student for nearly 20 more years. He was a “role model” for the school, said Michael Miles, banjoist and a longtime Old Town School teacher.
“He was very unassuming, quick with a smile, with lots of appreciation for everything and everybody around him. That sort of thing is what makes the Old Town School vital for so many people,” Miles said. “You’re coming here to take lessons but you’re coming back for the interpersonal experience you have with the people you meet there. It’s a countercultural place like no other, and Ted was a big part of that for all these years.”
Born in 1928, Johnson grew up in Evanston. While he earned his doctorate in American Literature at Northwestern University and taught at Michigan State, Indiana University, and Loyola University, his academic career was a cover for his ultimate passion: singing and performing music with others.
“He was a man made of music,” said Kate Thomas, his daughter. “My dad was curious his whole life. He was never disengaged. He was a lifelong learner in the whole sense. One of the things he loved learning was music. It was a whole language for him.”
Johnson sang in the high school choir. After graduation he frequented Downtown Chicago’s Gate of Horn, the first nightclub for folk music in the country. There he met folk stars of the era, from Odetta and Josh White and Theodore Bikel to Peggy Seeger and Frank Hamilton, the school’s first teacher and Gate of Horn house guitarist, and Ella Jenkins. Many became lifelong friends.
Today the Old Town School of Folk Music is headquartered at 4544 N. Lincoln Ave. in the Lincoln Square neighborhood.
Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Time
After a girlfriend gifted him with a guitar, he joined them. Soon enough he found himself teaching guitar in the living room of Oak Park resident Dawn Greening. Those sessions would serve as the inspiration for the school to open on the second floor of a labor hall in Old Town.
On opening night, Dec. 1, 1957, Hamilton demonstrated the unique teaching methodology to a group of Chicago notables, including Studs Terkel and notorious 43rd Ward alderman Paddy Bauler. Onstage was folk star Big Bill Broonzy, who performed bits of music that Hamilton would then notate on a blackboard.
Until then, learning an instrument meant having one-on-one instruction at a conservatory. What made the Old Town School’s method groundbreaking was that it was intentionally designed to make learning accessible to anyone, no matter their background or aptitude.
“A couple of minutes later, we played the riff. Transmitting this supposedly arcane thing for these ordinary people who had never done that before — it was really dramatic,” Johnson later told this writer.
After Hamilton, Johnson became the Old Town School’s second teacher. He taught guitar, banjo and, in the late 1990s, even yodeling after singers like Jewel and LeAnn Rimes re-introduced the vocal flourish to the pop charts. Johnson told the Chicago Tribune in 1998 that he learned how to yodel from his brother on a ski trip. “One thing about skiing is that you can get on the chair lift, practice yodeling, and no one can get at you,” he joked to the Tribune.
Johnson long credited the Old Town School for giving him a life outside music, too. He met his wife Marcia there in 1963. Their first date: singing together at the Drake Hotel where he had a gig. The couple would marry in 1966 and have two children; their son, Aaron, died in 1978.
While raising their children in Uptown, Johnson participated in many of the school’s programming in the neighborhoods including Project Upbeat, which in 1970 gave free guitars and instruction to 50 children in Old Town. Thomas remembered many folk luminaries staying in their apartment during her childhood, including Appalachian folk singer and guitarist Doc Watson.
“My dad really wanted people anywhere to pick up an instrument and play it, he didn’t think anyone needed classical training or needed to read music. He didn’t see music or music education as an enclave of the elite. He felt it should be open to people,” said Thomas. “The idea of getting together and playing an instrument was very important to him.”
Once Johnson retired from teaching, he decided to return to the Old Town School as a student. He studied Irish fiddle so he could join his two grandchildren in learning the instrument. He was also fundamental to helping popularize Shape Note, or Sacred Harp, singing throughout Chicago. The a cappella style of choral music is now performed throughout the city by different singing groups.
Johnson died Saturday at Rainbow Hospice located at Resurrection Hospital in Chicago. In the days before he passed, musicians visited to talk, listen or perform. articles.title: Lawsuits accuse Chicago delivery robot companies of collecting biometric data

Lawsuits accuse Chicago delivery robot companies of collecting biometric data - WBEZ Chicago
A Coco Robotics delivery robot sits parked outside KFire Korean BBQ located at 1241 N. Clybourn Ave. in the Old Town neighborhood, Wednesday, April 22, 2026. | Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times
Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Time
News
Chicago
Business
Lawsuits accuse Chicago delivery robot companies of collecting biometric data
The lawsuits center on two Chicago customers who allege that Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics collected their biometric data without their consent.
By
Misha Manjuran Oberoi
Updated
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Food delivery robots rolling along Chicago sidewalks are at the center of two lawsuits alleging the companies behind them are collecting customers’ biometric data without their consent.
The proposed class-action lawsuits, filed Oct. 9 in Cook County, accuse Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics of violating Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act by scanning customers’ faces and hands as they retrieve food orders, then retaining the data for artificial intelligence training and sharing it with third parties.
Both companies deny the allegations.
Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act, enacted in 2008, requires companies collecting biometric identifiers such as scans of face or hand geometry to provide written notice explaining the purpose and duration of collection and obtain written consent. The law also regulates how companies store and share the information.
The lawsuits center on two Chicago customers who say they were never told their biometric data was being collected. Mitchell Breidinger, a DoorDash customer, received a delivery from a Coco robot on Sept. 29, 2025, while Barry Schain, an Uber Eats customer, received three deliveries from Serve robots, most recently on Oct. 4, according to the filings.
The complaints allege the robots’ cameras and light detection and ranging, or LiDAR, sensors capture three-dimensional measurements of customers’ faces and hands when they approach the machines to unlock their compartments and retrieve their orders.
They also say the robots scan the faces, hands and bodies of other people they encounter on Chicago sidewalks.
The Coco complaint also alleges the company shares robot-collected data with OpenAI for artificial intelligence training. The complaint against Serve alleges the company licenses video and LiDAR data to third parties to train their own models.
Coco called the claims meritless, adding that privacy and compliance with privacy laws are a top priority for the company.
“This lawsuit fundamentally misunderstands our technology,” Carl Hansen, Coco’s head of government relations, said in a statement. “We have not collected biometric data in Chicago, and thus have never shared it with any third-parties, and are confident that this frivolous lawsuit will go away.”
A Serve Robotics spokesperson said the company would defend itself against the lawsuit, adding that its robots use cameras and sensors to navigate sidewalks safely.
“Serve does not use that data to identify individuals and our systems are not designed to identify individuals or create biometric profiles,” the spokesperson said.
The lawsuits seek statutory damages of $1,000 for each negligent violation of the biometric privacy act or $5,000 for each intentional or reckless violation, along with court orders requiring the companies to comply with the law and payment of attorney fees and costs.
The plaintiffs’ lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Chicago puts in bid to host 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup
articles.text:
Chicago puts in bid to host 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup - WBEZ Chicago
Brazil’s defender Thais Ferreira (No. 15) and US defender Emily Sams (No. 2) fight for the ball during the international women’s friendly football match between Brazil and the United States at the Neo Quimica Arena in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on June 6, 2026, ahead of the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup.
Miguel Schincariol/AFP via Getty
News
Money
Chicago
Chicago puts in bid to host 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup
While the Chicago Sports Commission would lead the charge, a spokesperson said Mayor Brandon Johnson’s office sent a letter of support of the initiative to the U.S. Soccer Federation earlier this month.
By
Violet Miller
Updated
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Chicago has once again put its hat in the ring to host a FIFA World Cup.
Mayor Brandon Johnson’s office wants the city to place a bid to be a host for the women’s competition in 2031, according to the office.
While the Chicago Sports Commission would lead the charge, a spokesperson said the mayor sent a letter of support of the initiative to the U.S. Soccer Federation on Oct. 7. The commission didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
A Johnson spokesperson said the bid process didn’t involve specifying any specific venue.
Chicago had previously passed twice on hosting the FIFA World Cup due to concerns of what it would cost taxpayers.
In 2010, Chicago dropped out of the United States’ unsuccessful bid to host the World Cup in either 2018 or 2022, when then-Mayor Richard M. Daley’s administration refused a promise to spend an estimated $10 million required to host matches.
Eight years later, under then-Mayor Rahm Emmanuel, Chicago once again dropped its bid to host the 2026 men’s tournament — despite Soldier Field making a short list for venues under consideration to host games — due to “uncertainty for taxpayers” regarding the cost for the city to host.
If Chicago were to host again, the most obvious venue would be Soldier Field. The stadium previously hosted the FIFA World Cup in 1994.
Since then, the stadium — which can pack in between 61,500 and 65,000 people depending on its configuration for football games or soccer matches — has consistently drawn crowds of more than 60,000 to see Lionel Messi play with Inter-Miami against the Chicago Fire. It has also hosted matches featuring Manchester United in recent years.
In April 2025, Messi played to a crowd of 62,538, and a slightly smaller crowd witnessed a 2023 game in Chicago he missed due to injury. The highest tally came just last month, when more than 63,000 fans packed Soldier Field.
Representatives for Soldier Field didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, nor did representatives from the Fire or Red Stars, Chicago’s National Women’s Soccer League team.
Another option could be hosting World Cup matches at the soon-to-be constructed McDonald’s Park that the Fire is building at The 78. That could put the event at a soccer-specific stadium projected to seat 22,000 when it opens in 2028.
In August, FIFA announced Maracaña Stadium in Rio de Janeiro would host the opening match and final of the 2027 Women’s World Cup. It is where the NFL recently made its South America debut at the renovated 79,000-seat stadium that hosted the 2014 men’s tournament.

Chicago man charged with grooming teen
Luis Gonzalez, 43, was charged with indecent solicitation of a child, grooming, and manufacturing harmful material, according to the Cook County Sheriff’s Office.
By

A Chicago man faces felony charges after he allegedly sent and solicited sexually explicit photos to a teenager, according to the Cook County Sheriff’s Office.
Luis Gonzalez, 43, is charged with indecent solicitation of a child, grooming, and manufacturing harmful material, the sheriff’s office announced Friday.
In June, the sheriff’s office received a tip that Gonzalez, who lives in Englewood, had illegal contact with a teenager. An investigation found Gonzalez sent sexually explicit photos and videos of himself to the teenage victim, and asked for similar images from the teen. Gonzalez also allegedly discussed having sex with the victim and encouraged the teen to sneak out to meet him, police said.
Gonzalez, who was arrested Tuesday, appeared in court Friday and was ordered detained at Cook County Jail.

The offices of four Democratic state representatives each received suspicious letters Friday.
Reps. Brad Schneider, Mike Quigley, Robin Kelly and Jan Schakowsky reported being sent the letters in a broader wave of threatening packages mailed to congressional and state election offices nationwide ahead of Election Day in November.
The reports come as similar suspicious mail has been sent to election officials and representatives in several states, including Louisiana, Ohio and Oklahoma, NPR reported.
Schneider’s office, which is located in Linconshire, contacted Lincolnshire and U.S. Capitol police after receiving the suspicious letter. It was ultimately deemed to not contain harmful substances by law enforcement.
Quigley’s office at 1925 N. Clybourn Ave. was also evacuated as a precaution Friday when a suspicious letter arrived there. Schakowsky’s Skokie office didn’t open the letter after warnings from the House sergeant-at-arms.
Schneider said the FBI is looking into the rash of threatening letters. The bureau didn’t immediately respond to a request for details on the investigation.
“It is imperative that [the FBI] follow all leads to apprehend and prosecute those responsible,” Schneider said in a statement. “Anyone or any group who thinks they can scare or intimidate Members of Congress or our teams from doing our job and work on behalf of the people we represent is sorely mistaken.”
Kelly said her team immediately contacted the U.S. Capitol Police, which she said is also investigating the incident. The police force didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
The Illinois State Board of Elections evacuated its offices Thursday when it received a suspicious letter, which was taken as part of the investigation by the FBI. A similar suspicious envelope containing baking powder was delivered to Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas’ downtown office at 118 N. Clark St. also on Thursday.
“Political violence has no place in a democracy, and efforts to scare or intimidate the public in the lead-up to an election must be resoundingly condemned,” Quigley said in a statement. “I hope that the perpetrator is swiftly brought to justice.”

Hilario Dominguez, a candidate for Chicago School Board president, spoke at a candidate forum in September. According to a report released Friday, the CPS inspector general’s office found there was insufficient evidence that Dominguez engaged in sexual misconduct in 2017 with a CPS student.

Insufficient evidence that Chicago School Board candidate engaged in sexual misconduct, watchdog report finds
The inspector general’s office defended its investigation following multiple calls for an independent review of how the district watchdog handled the matter so close to Election Day.
By
Kalyn Belsha and  Emmanuel Camarillo
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE

Chicago Public Schools’ watchdog determined there was insufficient evidence that Hilario Dominguez, a candidate for Chicago School Board president, engaged in sexual misconduct with a CPS student nearly a decade ago, in part because there were no eyewitnesses to the alleged behavior and her allegations did not point to a “sustained pattern of behavior.”
The 34-page report, obtained by WBEZ Friday through an open records request, notes that when the inspector general’s office first opened its case in 2021, it did so because CPS was notified that a Pilsen-based nonprofit had investigated Dominguez in 2018 for alleged conduct “that raised grooming concerns.”
But after interviewing the young woman who raised the allegations, investigators said the two incidents she recalled that made her feel uncomfortable in 2017, when she was 17 years old, were “less indicative of sexual misconduct” and “narrower in scope” than the internal report filed with the nonprofit.
The inspector general’s office said the woman alleged that Dominguez asked “about her dating preferences on one occasion” and physically picked her up “holding her body against his, and swinging her from side to side on another occasion.” After she complained to staff at The Resurrection Project, the nonprofit where she participated in a summer jobs program, Dominguez “never made her uncomfortable again.”
The reopened investigation, coming just weeks before voters head to the polls, has roiled the heated race for school board president. Dominguez, a former CPS teacher and former deputy political director for the Chicago Teachers Union, has denied the allegations and said they were surfaced by Aida Flores, a former political opponent who ran against him for a City Council seat in 2019.
The inspector general’s office said the upcoming election was not a factor in reopening the investigation, and that the young woman did not seem to have a political motive to first report the alleged behavior to The Resurrection Project in 2017.
The CPS watchdog reopened its investigation last month after the young woman, who is now 26, called that office and said she hadn’t known about the investigation and wanted a chance to speak with investigators.
“The political backdrop is relevant but should not distract from the question at the heart of this investigation: whether Dominguez attempted to groom [redacted name] for a sexual purpose or sexually harassed her,” the report states. “Given that those allegations were not otherwise corroborated by the evidence, the OIG did not have to consider the issue of political motivation to determine that the allegations against Dominguez are not substantiated.”
If the incidents did happen, the inspector general’s office wrote, it was also unclear if they were sexually motivated. The office said it’s possible the behavior the young woman described could have been “part of an ill-advised matchmaking effort or attempt to relate to her as a mentor.”
And while the alleged conduct, alongside the available evidence, didn’t meet the school district’s threshold for grooming or sexual harassment, the inspector general’s office said the alleged conduct would not be acceptable for a CPS staffer and noted that it would violate CPS’ current standards for boundaries between staff and students.
But those standards did not yet exist in 2017 and Dominguez was on a break from working at CPS at the time.
Earlier this week, Rima Kapitan, a lawyer for Dominguez, said the inspector general’s report “fully cleared” Dominguez of any wrongdoing.
Dominguez said in a statement on Wednesday that he now wants to “re-center his campaign” on education issues.
In a statement provided to WBEZ through her lawyer, the young woman said the process for investigating her claims had been “deeply flawed.”
“Like so many victims and survivors undermined by a broken system before me, I know what happened to me, and I am not going to be silenced,” she wrote. “While I am disappointed in the failure of this report to affirmatively verify my experience, it certainly does not exonerate Hilario Dominguez, or ‘clear him in full,’ as he claims.”
The inspector general’s office attempted to reach the young woman and her parents on 12 occasions in 2022, including leaving several voicemails for her mother and father as well as direct messages to the woman’s social media accounts, according to the report. It adds that the woman’s mother “would have been familiar with the OIG and would have been trained” on sexual misconduct investigation practices within CPS.
Additionally, investigators reviewed text messages that were “potentially inconsistent” with some of the young woman’s claims. She told the inspector general’s office that Dominguez had reached out to her on two occasions to set up a meeting in 2020 and 2022.
However, text messages show that it was the young woman, not Dominguez, who reached out for a meeting in 2022, including suggesting they meet alone. The meeting never took place.

articles.title: Cash floods CPS School Board races, with big money groups outraising the Chicago Teachers Union 5 to 1
articles.text:
Cash floods CPS School Board races, with big money groups outraising the Chicago Teachers Union 5 to 1 - WBEZ Chicago
Chicago School Board president candidates Jessica Biggs (from left), Hilario Dominguez and Victor Henderson, at a forum on Wednesday hosted by WBEZ, the Chicago Sun-Times and Chalkbeat Chicago.
Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times

Cash floods CPS School Board races, with big money groups outraising the Chicago Teachers Union 5 to 1
Billionaire-backed groups aligned against the Chicago Teachers Union are aiming their dollars toward attacking the CTU’s pick for school board president. But two weeks out, with its large membership, CTU could still make its mark.
By
Lauren FitzPatrick and  Sarah Karp
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share

Bluesky
Print
Back when the idea of an elected school board was still being debated, opponents voiced fears that the powerful Chicago Teachers Union would simply try to buy the elections.
Yet as Chicago stands on a historic precipice of electing all 20 members and a citywide president on Nov. 3 that’s not how it’s playing out.
Cash is flooding the election but the bulk so far has come from wealthy, often suburban donors, whose political groups have outraised the CTU 5:1 and outspent the teachers union nearly 3:1, according to an analysis of the most recent campaign finance filings between Oct. 1, 2025, and Oct. 15, 2026.
Charter school backers and a few prominent billionaires aligned in a shared antipathy for the teachers union have aimed their millions attacking the Chicago Teacher Union’s choice for board president rather than at bolstering any particular candidate, the Sun-Times/WBEZ analysis shows.
More than a quarter of the $8.1 million total spent on all races so far by these political action committees and the independent expenditure committees, known as super PACs, has targeted a single candidate: Hilario Dominguez.
The spending to oppose Dominguez is more than four times the amount spent on the top supported candidate, Jessica Biggs, one of the other two candidates for school board president.
Biggs, a former CPS principal, has attracted wide-ranging contributions from labor unions other than the CTU, former CPS leaders and investment bankers and CEOs — such as Michael Sacks of GCM Grosvenor and Paul Finnegan of Madison Dearborn Partners.
Both Biggs and Dominguez have directly raised about $1 million. Defense attorney Victor Henderson, who lent himself $500,000, trails in fundraising with no support from special interest groups, unions or PACs — something he touts.
Arnie Rivera, CPS former chief operating officer who heads a new advocacy group called the Chicago Education Alliance, said the billionaire-funded political groups see the school board races as an opportunity to take down the CTU before the mayoral race in February. Mayor Brandon Johnson remains closely allied with the union, which helped catapult their former organizer to office. Some of the $12.7 million raised by three education-focused political action committees spending big will almost certainly be deployed in the mayor’s race.
“It just becomes a proxy battle on the political side,” Rivera said. “CTU is a huge political group here in the city, and I think you have people who are trying to push back on it. I think that is what it comes down to.”
The latest campaign finance reports from the Illinois State Board of Elections, which were due by midnight Thursday, show an escalation of cash and spending in the last three months, both directly by the campaigns, as well as by outside groups on their behalf.
The 43 total candidates vying for board seats have directly raised another $4.1 million since the end of June, adding up to $5.9 million in contributions since October 2025. Since August, four candidates have withdrawn. There are also four write-in candidates.
Candidates just for the board president position account for $3.5 million, including contributions for two who recently dropped out.
Twenty local district races, 15 of which are contested, split the remaining $2.4 million. Eleven races have accumulated more than $100,000, with one competitive Northwest Side race in District 1b pulling in $292,062 in contributions.
None of the five district candidates running unopposed is aligned with the CTU. Current school board members Che “Rhymefest” Smith and Ellen Rosenfeld have raised $100,000 each.
“I’m open to taking money from anybody,” Smith said, noting that he also has gotten donations from SEIU, the union that represents support staff in CPS. “But I’ll tell you one thing that’s interesting: They never asked me to vote a certain way. They never have given a policy and said, ‘Push that through.’ ”
Chicago Board of Education member Che “Rhymefest” Smith, seen at a Board of Education meeting in 2025, has raised $100,000 for reelection, though he faces no opponent on the ballot.
Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times
Big money coming from a new outside group
The real money in these races is being raised and spent outside the campaigns via a series of political action committees and super PACs. The latter face no limits on how much they can raise or spend, as long as they don’t coordinate with candidates.
In addition to wealthy charter school supporters who typically amass and spend when school issues are at stake, billionaire Sacks has dropped millions attacking the Chicago Teachers Union candidates via his newly formed Common Ground Collective super PAC.
That group has spent the most so far, $3.7 million on digital ads and production, about half of it attacking Dominguez, a teacher-turned-CTU deputy political director.
The group has yet to endorse or fund ads in support of anyone for board president, though Sacks himself gave $400,000 to Biggs.
